messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marvin, a thirty‑year‑old African‑American curriculum designer, had once found comfort in the orderly cadence of lesson plans and the quiet hum of his office’s fluorescent lights. The life he had known—a single, focused professional life—was shattered that spring when a physical altercation with his then‑girlfriend turned his home into a scene of violence. The night of the attack, she struck him repeatedly in the ribs and jaw while drunk, her breath heavy with the stench of alcohol. He remembered the hot, acrid smell of burning plastic from the fire alarm that had blared moments earlier, the sharp sting of smoke on his tongue, and the sharp, metallic taste of blood on his lips. Those sensations were etched into his memory alongside the raw terror he felt, a terror that felt all the more real when the smoke was still in the air. The pain was not just psychological; he could feel the exact same ache in his ribs and jaw when the memory surfaced. A year later, Marvin began noticing that the scent of a colleague’s cologne—containing a faint hint of the same alcohol he had once inhaled—could suddenly trigger a flood of old memories. In meetings, when a coworker joked about family dinners, the words “family” landed like a hammer on his ears, pulling him back into the night of the assault. The combination of those family‑related comments and the lingering odor of alcohol in the office space forced his mind to relive the event, and each time the memory returned, the physical pain in his ribs and the panic that had driven him to the emergency room resurfaced with unnerving clarity. The very triggers that had been benign for years became the doorways to a painful past. The vividness of those memories did more than simply bring pain. As he recalled the night, the terror he once felt swelled into a full‑scale panic that left him trembling and heart racing. The same scenes that had once been confined to the darkness of that night now erupted whenever he smelled burnt plastic, smelled alcohol, or heard family gossip in the office corridor. Each time a trigger appeared, the memory rushed forward so forcefully that it seemed as though the past had leapt out of its temporal bounds and into his present, a loop that pulled him deeper into the same emotional landscape. Marvin’s struggle was not limited to the physical sensations of the memory. The recollection of the assault forced him to confront a new self‑image that he felt was utterly unrecognizable. He could no longer see the calm, dependable man who had designed curriculum and met deadlines; instead, he saw a man who felt forever dirty, as if the violent assault had smeared an invisible stain across his entire being. He was consumed by a sense of injustice, convinced that the world had failed him and that no one had done anything to right the wrong that had been inflicted upon him. The injustice, the contamination, and the alienation from his own identity fed into each other, creating a relentless cycle of self‑denigration that lingered long after the memory had faded. The same triggers that opened the floodgate to memory also amplified Marvin’s negative appraisals. Every time a coworker, in casual conversation, mentioned a family holiday or a mother’s anniversary, Marvin could not help but feel that these references were a reminder that his past had been discarded, that he was no longer the person he had once been. The presence of alcohol in the office, even if only a faint whiff, amplified his belief that he was forever tainted, that society had left him in the shadows of shame. The combination of these triggers and the weight of his negative thoughts made Marvin feel that he could never fully reintegrate into his professional sphere or rebuild the identity he had lost. Today, Marvin sits at his desk surrounded by stacks of worksheets and student feedback, the office hum a constant backdrop to his inner turmoil. He no longer feels at ease when a colleague speaks about their family, and the smell of after‑shave in the break room makes his chest tighten as though he were again on the brink of an assault. In the months since the assault, his productivity has slipped; he often arrives late to meetings, and his once‑reliable project deadlines have become sporadic. He has been avoiding conversations about family and has kept his personal life under wraps, a self‑imposed isolation that has left him feeling increasingly alienated from his own colleagues. It is this spiraling sense of being stuck, of never escaping the phantom presence of violence and the guilt of an unrecognizable self, that finally led him to seek help. He hopes to reclaim the calm that once guided his lesson plans, and he fears that if he does not break this cycle, he will forever live in the shadows of that night.
